results.ai_answer: Human somatic cells normally contain 46 chromosomes arranged as 23 pairs (22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes). This diploid chromosome number is essential for maintaining a stable genetic complement, with two copies of most genes providing redundancy and proper gene dosage. Accurate mitosis preserves this 46-chromosome set in daughter cells, while meiosis produces haploid gametes (23 chromosomes) so that fertilization restores the diploid number across generations. A correct chromosome number underpins normal embryonic and fetal development; deviations (aneuploidy such as trisomy 21, trisomy 18, trisomy 13, Turner syndrome, Klinefelter syndrome, or structural rearrangements) can cause developmental disorders, congenital anomalies, intellectual disability, infertility, and miscarriage. Abnormal chromosome number or structure in somatic cells is also a hallmark of many cancers, contributing to oncogene activation and loss of tumor suppressors. Because of this, chromosome analysis (karyotyping, microarray, genomic tests) is central to diagnosing developmental delay, reproductive problems, prenatal abnormalities, and malignancies, highlighting the fundamental significance of the normal 46-chromosome complement for human development and genetic health.
